events.title: Corgi girls, ugly lawsuits, and doggy drama: Inside a wild $5 billion startup
events.summary: Emily Yuan and Nico Laqua, cofounders of Corgi PR Newswire "If you can't raise a dog, you cannot run an office." That was the message Nico Laqua , cofounder and CEO of buzzy insurance startup Corgi , sent to staff in the New York office about one of the company's short-legged mascots. A vet had told the employees that the puppy, Hamilton, should not be outside because he wasn't fully vaccinated, so they were using pee pads in the office. After Laqua, based in San Francisco, heard that workers were not walking Hamilton, he laid down the law in a July 19 missive. "Buying pee pads of any sort for Hamilton is a fireable office [sic], on the spot," he wrote in the message. Those who refused to take the corgi to the street should book a one-on-one. "The best case scenario for this meeting will be a PIP," he said, using shorthand for the disciplinary process known as a performance improvement plan. It's hard to imagine this kind of C-suite drama playing out at Liberty Mutual, Berkshire Hathaway, or other giants of the buttoned-up commercial underwriting industry. But Corgi is decidedly not your granddaddy's insurance company. The CEO is loudly online, bragging his way across X while communicating with his staff on the messaging app Telegram . A squad of young women dubbed "Corgi girls" relentlessly promotes the company and their own hot takes on social media. It recently embarked on a massive expansion of a curious side hustle: a chain of 24-hour Corgi cafes. The startup is constantly announcing new products and ventures; it has an exchange-traded funds arm, a plaintiff's legal firm, and file-sharing software, but the core product is insurance. Corgi markets its startup business insurance in the forefront, and offers the usual options, too: insurance for your apartment, your truck, your bar. "We want to be a one-stop shop," Jeremy Eisemann, senior vice president, told Business Insider. The frenetic pace carries over to its financials. It's raised over $431 million; in May, it announced a $106 million round three weeks after a $160 million unicorn round. The company is now valued at $5 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter. Haden Kirkpatrick, a longtime insurance tech advisor and investor who is not involved in Corgi's business, said he'd never seen an insurance company raise money like it. "The companies that hold risk in this space — that actually have a premium on paper that they have to reserve against — don't come anywhere near that," he said. The raises impressed Kirkpatrick, who said he understands why investors were excited. Corgi had that Silicon Valley ethos. "If you're a technology company, you're at warp speed," he said. "If you're an insurer, you're crawling." Business Insider spoke with current and former employees, analysts, investors, and prospective customers about Corgi's trajectory, and reviewed dozens of documents. One thing was clear: Corgi is speedrunning in a sleepy sector. Some say it's disrupting a business that needs a shake-up. Others caution it's been tried before: Lemonade , Hippo , and Root vowed in the 2010s to upend the status quo, then fizzled. "It's not so much that they failed and went away," said Nathan Golia, a senior analyst at Celent. "It's that the idea that insurance was ripe to be picked off by a tech company turned out to not really be correct." Corgi's insurance business for startups is at the forefront of its mission. Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Neither of Corgi's cofounders had insurance experience. They knew how to make Roblox games. Laqua, now 26, met Emily Yuan during her sophomore year at Stanford, before she dropped out. They created the social app Picnic and scaled it into the gaming studio Basket Entertainment, earning glossy magazine stories and a spot on the Forbes "30 Under 30" list. After they got into the startup accelerator Y Combinator , Laqua and Yuan obtained insurance licenses and launched Corgi in 2024. The new company quickly spent $30 million on YRIG, an Alabama-based tenant liability insurance company, according to people familiar with the matter. "How do you buy a $30M insurance carrier with just $500K from YC?" Jared Friedman , a YC partner, said in an investor's blog post . "It seems impossible. And yet, Nico and Emily pulled it off." YRIG isn't a traditional insurance agency but a risk retention group. Corgi also operates through the Arizona-based risk retention group TRRG. That means if Corgi were to fail, policyholders under YRIG and TRRG wouldn't be guaranteed payouts by the state. Corgi said that the company operates through many insurers, including admitted or fully licensed carriers, and that RRGs are "industry standard for certain types of risks." YRIG is also unrated, and Corgi said it does not plan to seek a rating for it. Corgi's Eisemann said the unrated status didn't diminish customer trust and that Corgi has more than enough funds to meet operational requirements. "We will be there when a covered claim is filed," he said. "The money is on the balance sheet. We have it sitting in the bank." Corgi grew its ranks quickly, opening eight offices, including San Francisco, Atlanta, Salt Lake City, Chicago, Dallas, New York, and London. It now has about 400 employees. Former employees of Corgi, which has a seven-day workweek, describe a hyper-competitive culture. Throughout the day, Laqua uses Telegram to rank workers and offices against each other on who has performed the most insurance demos, messages seen by Business Insider show. Laqua told Business Insider that it has a "bot that tracks revenue activity, like most companies do." The sales team's approach isn't always appreciated, based on social media posts by prospective customers complaining about an onslaught of calls, texts, and even FaceTime outreach. Ari Ramdial, the San Francisco-based founder of the stablecoin wallet Guap, thought Corgi's coverage might be a fit for his startup. Seconds after entering his information on the company's site in May, his phone began blowing up with calls and texts from employees — a startling deluge even for a sales-based industry. "At one point, I was getting two calls from two different Corgi numbers simultaneously," he told Business Insider. He responded to one email, saying it was "incredibly annoying," and requested that they "please stop calling me repeatedly." A Corgi rep responded by apologizing and offering an "apology gift," which he did not accept. Asked about Ramdial's complaint, Corgi told Business Insider that "customers appreciate responsiveness," and that those who ask not to be contacted are put on a no-call list. i signed up for Corgi out of curiosity after seeing their fundraise announcement. tell me why i got bombarded with 6 calls and 5 text messages all from different people within a 1 minute time span. yikes https://t.co/cqONSnvpzn pic.twitter.com/lXgjNqtVW7 — ari ramdial (@ariramdial) May 28, 2026 Corgi's sales pitches to potential clients have also been th

events.title: Turkiye arrests president, six members of football refereeing body in probe
events.summary: Arrests were made over interference with refereeing procedures, among other accusations, Turkish justice minister says. The head of Turkiye’s football refereeing body and six other people have been arrested over accusations of interference in refereeing procedures, Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said. “Claims regarding interference in the formation of referee classifications, assignments, scoring and appointment processes, as well as rule examinations, have been investigated,” Gurlek wrote in a social media post on Tuesday. Ferhat Gundogdu, the president of the refereeing body, and his deputy were among those arrested. Gurlek said searches had been carried out at the suspects’ “residences, workplaces and offices”. “We will steadfastly continue the fight for clean football so that claims undermining trust in Turkish football are clarified, those responsible are held accountable before the law, and football is remembered for the effort, struggle, and sportsmanship on the field,” Gurlek added. A year ago, the Turkish Football Federation (TFF) suspended 149 referees on charges of involvement in an illegal betting scandal . The TFF investigation found that 371 out of the country’s 571 referees officiating in the professional leagues had betting accounts and 152 of them actively placed bets. Some 29 people were arrested in the sprawling scandal, including 14 footballers, one of whom was Fenerbahce’s international midfielder Mert Hakan Yandas. Authorities suspended more than 1,000 players, including 25 from the first division. However, Gurlek did not draw any link between last year’s betting scandal and the current investigation.

events.title: Iranians stock up on food and medicine as fears of new US fighting grow
events.summary: Stockpiling and calls for military action are among signs of increasing precarity as economy conditions worsen. Tehran, Iran – Iranians are stocking up on food and medicines as fears grow that the country will face dire shortages as the United States tightens an embargo on the country. The Iranian government had managed to keep household staples flowing during the early months of the war. But a US naval blockade and pivot to draconian sanctions have led to fears that imports will be limited. list 1 of 3 Iran touts Hormuz attacks as oil flows increase despite tensions list 2 of 3 Flights between Iran and Iraq’s Najaf resumes amid US aviation sanctions list 3 of 3 Iran’s Araghchi meets Qatari mediators as US calls for nuclear talks More recently, the US announced a ban on Iranian airlines worldwide and is pressing other countries to cut trade ties with Iran in a bid to isolate the country. Addressing the United Nations General Assembly last week, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian condemned Washington for its blockade on his country, saying it will prevent food and medicine from reaching the Iranian people. On Saturday, US President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s offer for a seven-day truce that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for economic relief and other conditions. As the war enters its eighth month and hopes for a diplomatic solution dim, Al Jazeera looks at how some Iranians are faring under a US embargo. Tehran’s stores remain stocked, but shoppers are keeping an eye on shop shelves. Their anxiety has deepened since a flurry of social media posts urging people to ensure they have several days of food before a possible new round of fighting with the US. At one shopping centre, Ali, 51, was loading a trolley packed with rice, flour, pasta, pulses, cooking oil and canned food. He is stocking up because he is convinced that Iran’s adversary is seeking to “starve” the people to push them to turn on their government. “This is not a war in the traditional sense. It targets the people to put pressure on the authorities,” he said. With flights to some nearby countries suspended, imports of certain medicines and mobile phone headsets are hard to find. The prices of those still available in shops have been pushed up. Haj Pasandideh, a 71-year-old grocer, said he believed warehouses were well-stocked with basic goods at the moment. But the problem lies in the daily price increases due to Iran’s weakening rial, prompting him to bulk-buy goods before the expected hikes. He sometimes caps cooking oil at one bottle per sale to ensure as many customers can purchase the goods as possible. Farmers are also on edge due to the embargo, unable to ship out their produce and forced to sell to local markets. The war has worsened the economic situation, even after years of sanctions that have pushed the country from being a regional exporter of agricultural and food products to being one of the region’s main importers. Mehran, an apple grower, told Al Jazeera that due to the difficulties of exporting, he had sold only a third of this year’s harvest, all of it inside Iran. Some neighbouring countries have halted trade with Iran in recent months, he said, while trucks now spend days at crossings they once cleared in a day, causing fruit to spoil before it reaches buyers. “The blockade has not only closed the sea and air but also the land routes but in an undeclared manner,” he said. The war has also deepened an already-dire shortage of medications . Some pharmacies Al Jazeera visited in southern Tehran had run out of infant formula and dozens of other types of medications. Although officials have assured Iranians that substitute products were available, pharmacy staff expressed concern about the increasing number of customers searching for infant formula in vain. “Imported medicines are disappearing fast, and lately people have been coming in to buy certain items before they need them for fear they will run out in future,” Mahsa, a 23-year-old pharmacy assistant, told Al Jazeera. She said the health authorities had introduced “smart systems” to track the quantity and type of medication each person buys. The prospect of a prolonged siege and deteriorating economic conditions have driven some Iranians to call for a military solution. On Tehran’s main thoroughfare, several people told Al Jazeera that another round of fighting with the US was unavoidable. Some urged the government to break the blockade by force before it is tightened further. Mohsen, a 23-year-old economics student, believes Washington’s goal is to strangle the Iranian economy and the cost will ultimately be felt by Iranian citizens. Iran possesses many strong cards that it must use to break the air and sea blockade before they develop into a land blockade that would completely choke Tehran, he said. Alireza Taghavinia, an Iranian international relations expert, told Al Jazeera that the gap between Washington and Tehran was too wide to be bridged.

events.title: The gut-check questions every leader needs to ask before building with AI
events.summary: There’s an idea gaining traction in enterprise technology: companies can save millions by using AI to build their own software. Forget buying a platform like SAP , Workday, or HubSpot . Instead, CIOs and their teams are creating custom apps with Claude Code and other tools. I get the appeal because I spent years in the CIO seat. Earlier in my career, the chairman of a beverage company I was working for asked my team to build a custom analytics dashboard. We had the talent. We had the resources. We figured, why not? Four months later and setback after setback, we had to confront a harder question: Even if we could build it, should we? Every month we spent building it was time my team wasn’t spending on other priorities that could create more value for the company. So we killed the project and bought a solution from a software company.  Fast-forward to today and I’m on the other side of the equation — I’m now a leader at a global software company that helps huge enterprises manage workflows for HR, customer service, finance, and more. I interact everyday with customers who are debating building their own software with AI or working with us. They know I have a product to sell. They also turn to me because they trust my expertise and experience on the ground. My advice: there are times to leverage AI to build your own software, but there are also cases where leaning on outside expertise and buying software is a no-brainer. Before taking the plunge, it’s worth asking a few questions to figure out whether building or buying software is right for you. Your company’s prospects, not to mention your own job as CIO, could be on the line.  1. Is this your company’s core competency?  At first glance, building instead of buying software might look like an easy call. You have all the engineering talent you need to crank out an app or platform, and the team is raring to go. But is building software a smart move, or does it steal cycles from your core competency? I see this with some of the most sophisticated engineering organizations in the world. One of our customers, a global technology company with hundreds of thousands of employees, has no shortage of people who know how to build stuff. Instead of wrestling with creating in-house software for billing and HR, however, they decided to keep their focus on innovation.  For any business today, even high-tech players, it’s all about leaning into your expertise, not building something totally unrelated to your business.   2. How much are you really saving?  For CIOs looking to build software, the savings pitch usually starts with the recurring subscription they’ll cut. In some enterprises, that could mean millions of dollars a year. But this doesn’t account for what it costs to develop, run, and maintain the replacement. For context: Depending on how complex their business is, we’ve seen that companies building their own LLM-based software solution will typically spend five to 10 times more than using our workflow automation platform.  Initial development costs are only the tip of the iceberg. Maintenance is the real expense, as well as the ongoing cost of keeping it secure, current, and running as the business changes.  I’ve seen this math play out firsthand. At a large financial services company, the CISO wanted to use an LLM to rewrite a core system. That process could easily take 18 to 24 months, all to save the equivalent of 0.5% of the company’s annual operating budget. 3. Have you factored in security and governance?  Getting software to work properly is tough enough. For companies that choose to build it, security and governance is a whole other ballgame with massive risks. Cybersecurity in the AI era has never been more complex, and the stakes have never been higher. Building something that works on day one isn’t a problem. The real test is defending it on day 1,000. Even when there’s no ill intent, your own AI agents can go rogue, doing exponential damage before anyone notices. Roughly half of orgs have seen AI agents exceed their permissions. Take car rental management platform PocketOS, which got its production database wiped by a coding agent in nine seconds. That’s why it’s critical that CIOs do an honest assessment of their team’s capabilities. Is your platform secure in the face of evolving threats? Is it auditable if regulators come knocking? Are you prepared to track permissions? Can you ensure your software complies with shifting regulations and requirements?  4. What happens when your CIO leaves?  There’s another question I’ve started asking in every build vs. buy conversation: What happens when your CIO leaves?  The average tenure for CIOs is about 4.5 years . A custom platform typically takes two or more years to build and longer to mature. The person who designed it, who made the architectural decisions, who knows where every integration lives, may very well be gone before the system is actually running well. A CIO I spoke with recently described a prior job where her predecessor had built a custom platform the entire organization depended on. When he left, so did the institutional knowledge. No documentation. No support team. No vendor to call. Just senior leaders staring at something they couldn’t explain and couldn’t afford to shut down. 5. Can you tap into proprietary data and institutional knowledge? All that said, building software rather than buying makes sense in the right contexts.  A CDIO I know at one of the world’s biggest shipping and logistics companies took this approach. He’s building in-house with AI, but being very intentional about where he puts resources. He only greenlights projects that differentiate the business and tap into its “secret sauce” — harnessing decades of internal data and other institutional knowledge to optimize shipping routes. And he also knows when to leverage AI by buying from a vendor. Putting AI-powered platforms to work on your existing workflows — like onboarding new employees or processing time-off requests — is a great place to start. These workflows might not be sexy, but they have clear guardrails and offer a direct path to ROI.   AI has made it easier than ever to build. It hasn’t eliminated the need to choose where you should. I’ve sat on both sides of the table — as the CIO eager to build his own software, and now as a president at a company that sells software. The decision to build or buy isn’t always an easy one, but for CIOs today that choice may be more important than ever and is worth careful consideration.  The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune . events.title: Reco raises $55M as AI agent security startups crowd the market
events.summary: Last day to demo your breakthrough to 10,000+ tech leaders is on Oct 2 . Book Exhibit Table Now. Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Terms like “AI sprawl” have become common fare on tech social media and in thought leadership as enterprises start deploying AI agents en masse. But CISOs worried about securing swarms of agents suddenly operating across networks are likely finding themselves dealing with a new kind of sprawl: vendors offering to help. Just a quick glance at public Crunchbase and PitchBook profiles turns up at least two dozen companies selling some form of AI agent security. Some vendors vet the tools agents use , while others try to help companies control what data their agents can reach . Some others, like CrowdStrike , are building detection and response controls on the devices agents run, and still others are focused on finding and resolving unapproved AI usage . The products differ, of course, but their promises to discover and govern agents sound quite similar, involving knowledge graphs, continuous monitoring, runtime security, tool access, MCP vetting, and the like. Some are even updating their products to join the bandwagon. Until last year, AI security startup Reco was mostly selling software to map and secure SaaS and AI platforms. Now, it’s repositioned around a broader solution that uses a context graph to connect agents to apps, people, accounts, and permissions, giving security teams a way to see what an agent can reach and cut off access it doesn’t need. According to Reco’s co-founder and CEO Ofer Klein, the biggest change over the past year that spurred the startup to broaden its scope was that companies are building and deploying AI agents faster than they can keep track of. At one of the startup’s Fortune 100 customers, he said, Reco’s platform found 21,000 agents the company didn’t know about. And at a large financial services customer, the startup claims it identified an agent set up by an ex-employee that could access Salesforce and share that data with a domain the company couldn’t see. “The market demand right now for agent security is not only about the agent itself; it’s about the entire ecosystem end-to-end,” Klein told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. Klein’s not alone in stressing the urgency for companies to secure this sprawl. Security startup HiddenLayer ‘s co-founder and CEO, Chris Sestito, earlier this month told me that when agents reach production, the scale of their costs and risk goes from theoretical to “full scale really quickly,” and that over 50 of his customers have AI agents in production touching critical systems and sensitive assets. Cymphony, another AI startup, said at one U.S. public company, it found about 85,000 files that had become accessible to AI tools and agents. There’s no doubt a ton of investors are interested in companies that can make a mint out of helping companies find and secure all these agents, and Reco has capitalized on that demand: The startup on Tuesday said it raised $55 million, building on a $30 million Series B in February . AT&T, a customer, invested in the extension via its venture arm, as did Forestay and Quadrille Capital. Klein said the company’s valuation has “more than doubled” since the Series B was first announced in February, and vaguely estimated it in the “high hundreds of millions” though he wouldn’t share specifics. Annual recurring revenue right now is in the “double-digit millions of dollars,” he said, and he expects it to triple this year. The startup has more than 100 customers, and financial services companies account for about 40% of the business. Reco’s bet, it appears, is that its existing coverage of SaaS apps, and the AI agents they are increasingly offering, will help it stand out from the crowd. The company currently integrates with more than 280 apps, and Klein says new integrations can be added within days. Klein said the platform uses browser and network signals to find agents outside apps it connects to directly within companies, and it has controls to inspect prompts and tool calls. The startup will use the new funding for hiring, sales, partnerships, and customer support. The new funding brings Reco’s total capital raised to $140 million. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Economists turn stock movements into an estimate of anticipated gains – while warning that markets can get carried away AMD bets $8.2B that worlds matter more than words in AI 15 hours ago AWS needs to embrace its place as the Home Depot of AI infrastructure 16 hours ago French dev aims to solve bots' blindness so they can understand GUIs 19 hours ago Open source datacenters and open source thinking will undo self-inflicted DC damage 1 day ago Big AI's content problem: Take the work, keep the money 2 days ago Investors appear to be betting that AI will deliver substantial gains in software engineering productivity, according to economists who used stock market movements to estimate the technology's expected impact. Economists affiliated with the University of California, Berkeley (UCB) and the London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) say that between November 2022 and December 2025, "AI increased the market's expected present value of software engineering productivity by the equivalent of a permanent 32.6 percent productivity increase." Alex Blumenfeld (UCB), Jonathon Hazell (LSE), Chen Lian (UCB), and Andreas Schaab (UCB) describe their findings in a National Bureau of Economics Research paper titled "The Macroeconomic Effect of AI: Sizing the Software Engineering Channel." The authors argue that investors have increasingly priced anticipated gains from AI development tools into company valuations since the introduction of ChatGPT in November 2022. "We empirically measure whether firms with larger software engineering payroll shares experience larger stock-price increases when the AI stock index rises," explained Chen Lian, assistant professor of finance at UC Berkeley, in an email to The Register . "We then use an economic model to translate that relationship into the AI-driven software engineering productivity gains investors anticipate. "A preliminary look at our data suggests that total software engineering employment among the firms covered has increased over the past few years. But our productivity estimate does not depend on that employment trend at all." Rather than measuring developers' output directly, the researchers examined how company stock returns respond to news about AI and whether that response varies with the proportion of each company's payroll devoted to software engineering. "By 'news about AI,' we mean new information reflected in stock prices," explained Lian. "As discussed above, we combine empirical measurements with an economic model to infer how AI has changed investors' expectations of software engineering productivity and the implied GDP impact." Lian acknowledges that market expectations may not fully materialize. "Our estimates capture the market’s assessment of current and future productivity gains, and markets can be overly optimistic or pessimistic," he said. "The advantage is a forward-looking measure, available in real time, when many of AI's effects have yet to play out." The market-implied productivity gain of 32.6 percent is comparable in magnitude to the 21-56 percent acceleration on individual tasks reported by other researchers, the authors say. They note however that task-level gains can be offset by bottlenecks that limit productivity gains. In the context of software development that might take the form of code reviews that can't keep pace with surging commit figures. Feeding the estimated productivity gain into their economic model also produces a sizeable implied effect on GDP. "News about AI from November 2022 to December 2025 corresponds to a present-value GDP increase equivalent to a permanent 3.61 percent level increase," the authors report. As to whether the productivity gains seen in software engineering are extensible to other industry sectors, Lian said: "Our methods can be used to study the economic impact of AI through other channels, which we plan to explore in follow-up work.

events.title: A YouTuber says this Muse setting led to the AI agent sharing his address: 'Be careful'
events.summary: A YouTuber says a misunderstood Muse setting turned a keyboard sale into an unexpected doorstep visit. Cheng Xin/Getty Images Matt Robb, a YouTuber, said Muse gave his address to a Facebook Marketplace buyer without his knowledge. Robb said Meta has since explained what happened: he had clicked an "Allow Always" setting. "Take care everyone, and double-check what permissions AI has in your life," Robb said. A YouTuber who said his Muse AI agent gave out his home address without his permission has got to the bottom of what happened — and it comes down to clicking one button. Matt Robb said in a Tuesday update on X that he had selected an "Allow Always" option when he first asked Meta's AI agent to sell his computer keyboard on Facebook Marketplace, believing it would still seek his approval before accepting offers. "It didn't, so be careful," Robb wrote. Instead, Robb said, the setting allowed Muse to send messages on his behalf using a template containing the pickup address he had previously supplied. A Marketplace buyer later showed up at his building after Muse accepted a $600 offer and exchanged messages with him without Robb's knowledge , he said. "I didn't think it would send it out to everyone that gave me an offer," Robb wrote. "It's worth checking." Robb said he spoke with Meta's Muse team, which reviewed the logs with him and said it would make the permission prompt clearer to avoid any misunderstanding. In a reply to Robb's Tuesday post, David Singleton, a Meta Superintelligence Labs staffer, said that Meta had confirmed there was "no breach of privacy controls." "We appreciate the opportunity to learn from your experience with Muse and keep making it better for everyone!" Singleton added. 'Double-check what permissions AI has in your life' The episode is an example of the growing pains facing the buzzy yet nascent personal AI agent market. Tools like Muse and Instinct promise to book trips , sift through inboxes, and complete online errands on behalf of the user. However, there's a tradeoff : they require access to accounts, payments, messages, and personal information. Early users are still working out what permissions to grant and how closely to supervise agents, amid reports of unintended actions, hallucinations, and security concerns. Over the weekend, Robb said in a viral post that Muse had accepted a lowball offer for a keyboard, shared his address, and communicated with the buyer when he arrived at Robb's building — all without his knowledge. So muse handled my Facebook marketplace today. Just found out it told people my address and agreed a lowball price and then they showed up without it even telling me until late tonight that it messed up. Absolutely wild. pic.twitter.com/F3ZhEO4unM — Matt Robb (@MattRobbt) September 27, 2026 In Tuesday's update, Robb said Meta also told him that a separate display error had made a $600 offer appear to have been accepted, even though he had set a minimum price of $700. The glitch removed the "7" from the message displayed to the buyer, he said, making Muse's response — "Sounds good, 00 it is!" — appear to confirm the lower price. Singleton said in his reply that Meta had fixed the "00" price-display issue. Robb suggested that Meta add a "Sent By Muse" label beneath each agent-generated message so recipients can distinguish AI-generated messages from those sent by a human. "There was really no way of knowing who sent what in the chat, which is very concerning," he wrote. Robb said he and the buyer resolved the mix-up, and the buyer later came by to purchase another item. His takeaway for other early adopters: "Take care everyone, and double-check what permissions AI has in your life." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The data center buildout is driving blue-collar job growth
events.summary: Data center construction spending is expected to grow. George Frey/Bloomberg via Getty Images Data centers aren't just powering your new favorite agent; they're also a key construction driver. The AI buildout is set to become the largest capital expenditure project in US history, dwarfing railroads and highways. Overall construction spending has fallen year-over-year, while data center spending has skyrocketed. Data centers are powering your chat ramblings — and the growth in the American construction industry. AI buildouts are set to become the largest capital expenditure project in US history, per a Brookings Institution analysis, outpacing spending on highways and railroads as a share of GDP. That massive spending and construction boom needs workers to — literally — prop it up. And blue-collar employment for data centers is booming, with the number of nonresidential specialty trade contractors — workers like electricians in non-residential buildings, which includes data centers— growing by 86,000 in the past year. "I think it's fair to say that a very large portion of construction labor demand right now is being driven by increasing data center construction activity," said Zach Fritz, an economist at Associated Builders and Contractors. Are you in a data center-related job? Reach out to these reporters to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com and jkaplan@businessinsider.com . The American Institute of Architects found, based on multiple forecasts of nonresidential construction, that data center construction spending is set to climb more than other kinds and account for about 8% of nonresidential building spending by 2027. But the sustainability of that jobs boom could be precarious. Construction spending on the whole has fallen 3.8% year-over-year as of July, according to the Census Bureau, and KPMG finds that data centers are a "structural growth driver" for spending. Year-over-year spending on data centers has grown by just over 57%, a sharp contrast to both residential and non-residential private spending growth since early 2025. For now, the data center boom is good news for construction workers and larger industry spending. Guy Berger, a senior fellow at the research organization Burning Glass Institute, said one concern is if the data center boom cycle ends up being shorter than anticipated: "And all of a sudden, we trained a lot of electricians, people like that, to do stuff that is no longer needed," Berger said. Data center workers are in demand Job postings on Indeed for data center-related roles have skyrocketed, up almost 130% from about two years ago, while overall postings are down compared with the same period. About half of the data-center demand this year came from the IT infrastructure, operations, and support occupational group and the installation and maintenance occupational group. A job-posting analysis from Lightcast, a job market intelligence company, showed a rise in demand for some data-center-related jobs. Based on growth in average monthly job postings from January to August 2022 and the same period this year, postings for electrical engineers within the utilities sector have increased 34%, and 22% for project management specialists. Within commercial and institutional building construction, there's been a rise in demand for construction managers, project management specialists, cost estimators, and civil engineers. And so, in the short term, the data center boom will likely remain a workhouse for the construction industry. What's more unclear is the longer-term prognosis, especially since AI infrastructure is still reliant on a slice of hardcore spenders to keep it afloat. "The next few years, it's stable. It's going to keep growing. We're going to keep building data centers," Fritz said. But rising community opposition could eventually limit the rate of growth, he said, or technological advancements might require smaller footprints. "There's all kinds of things that could happen here," he said. "They're not going to happen anytime soon." It's unclear how permanent data center jobs will ultimately be, especially after data center construction, but listings on Indeed at least suggest firms are advertising them as long-term. Aubrey Woessner, an economist at Indeed Hiring Lab, said only about two in every 1,000 data center postings are temporary. "'Permanent' is a label the employer chooses, and there's reason to think it may overstate how durable these roles really are: Local incentive agreements often require a project to create a set number of permanent positions, which gives employers a reason to post that way regardless of how long a given build-out job actually lasts," Woessner said. events.title: M&S links up with Sephora to lure younger shoppers
events.summary: Beauty specialist will open branded areas in 100 Marks & Spencer stores and will sell its products on chain’s website Marks & Spencer has signed a deal with Sephora to open areas under the beauty brand’s name within its stores, in its latest tactic to attract younger shoppers. The French retailer is to launch branded areas staffed by Sephora employees in 100 M&S stores and sell through the British retailer’s website in spring next year. Sephora relaunched in the UK in 2023 with huge fanfare and now has about 18 stand-alone British stores. The company is owned by LVMH, the luxury goods group led by Bernard Arnault, who with his family is among the world’s richest people with a $171bn (£129bn) fortune, according to Forbes. The company has rapidly expanded on its second attempt to enter the UK market after closing a handful of stores in 2005, having failed make a dent in a competitive sector. The deal with M&S marks a new strategy in its expansion plans. Analysts have said Sephora’s work with up-and-coming brands and collaborations with high-profile influencers on Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube has helped the company reach its target female audience of 24- to 36-year-olds. John Lyttle, the managing director of M&S’s fashion, home and beauty division, said: “Beauty is an important category for M&S, with the potential to attract new customers to shop with us and give existing customers the opportunity to shop with us more often.” “Combining Sephora’s specialist expertise with the strength of the M&S brand, our store estate and our growing digital platform,” Lyttle said. “Alongside this, we will continue investing in our own-label beauty categories where we have established strength and customer trust.” Retailers have been battling to grab a share of the beauty market after the disappearance of many department stores. In recent years a swathe of UK department stores have closed, including Debenhams, Beales and about half the House of Fraser chain. Sephora’s self-service model – which allows consumers to touch and test makeup and perfume without the help of shop staff – is seen to appeal to younger shoppers, who may test in store and buy online. The tie-up could provide increased competition for the specialist health and beauty chains Boots and Superdrug. Lyttle said the deal was part of M&S’s wider transformation plan, which involves £700m of investments in revitalising stores, modernising its supply chain and distribution system, and further improvements in products. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning The group, which employs more than 65,000 people, has 227 full-line stores – containing food, clothing, homewares and beauty – after closing dozens of old and out-of-place outlets. More will shut over the next two years and a handful of new outlets are opening with the aim to have 200 full-line stores in the UK. M&S’s food arm is expanding rapidly, with 18 food-only stores opening this year as it heads for a target of 420, compared with 335 directly operated outlets. Franchise partners run another 466 in the UK and more overseas. Sarah Boyd, the managing director of Sephora UK, said: “Together, we can redefine what high street beauty means for customers across the UK, bringing the very best curated brand and beauty experience to the M&S stores.” She said the group would introduce its beauty advisers to M&S stores to “provide a truly personalised experience, and to reach customers in more communities where they already live, shop and spend their time”.

events.title: IRS sends notices on Saver's Match to taxpayers who might qualify for new benefit, worth up to $2,000
events.summary: The Saver's Match program, which was authorized in 2022 Secure 2.0 retirement legislation, will provide income-eligible retirement savers with a matching annual contribution worth up to $1,000 for single filers and $2,000 for joint filers beginning with the 2027 tax year. The IRS sent CP321J notices to taxpayers who claimed the saver's credit — which the Saver's Match will replace — on their 2025 returns or whose 2025 income would make them eligible. The Treasury Department and the IRS plan to issue regulations to govern the operation of the Saver's Match and are seeking input from the public until Oct. 5 to address potential complications in the program. The IRS has begun notifying some taxpayers who may be eligible for a new retirement cash contribution debuting next year. Authorized by the 2022 Secure 2.0 retirement legislation, the upcoming Saver's Match program will provide income-eligible retirement savers with a matching annual contribution worth up to $1,000 for single filers and $2,000 for joint filers beginning with the 2027 tax year. According to a recent post on the IRS website, the agency sent CP321J notices to taxpayers who claimed the saver's credit — which the Saver's Match is replacing — on their 2025 tax return or whose 2025 income was otherwise in the range of eligibility. The IRS did not respond to a CNBC email asking how many taxpayers received the notice. As Republicans tout Trump's 'big beautiful bill,' here's who the tax breaks benefited IRS tax debt agreements have plummeted: 'I've never seen a number that low' New Social Security bill would lower retirement age to 60 for some workers Fed rate hike squeezes younger and lower-income households CNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms ranked CNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026 The benefit is available whether workers save through a workplace plan like a 401(k) or in an individual retirement account. People would claim the Saver's Match with a new Form 8880-A when filing their 2027 tax return in 2028, according to the IRS. Before the Saver's Match takes effect, the saver's credit remains available through the 2026 tax year for lower- and moderate-income retirement savers. It's also worth up to $1,000 for single filers and $2,000 for joint filers who contribute to their retirement accounts, depending on income. But it's a nonrefundable tax credit, meaning it can only reduce your tax bill to $0, rather than generate a refund. "The Saver's Match will very likely be more effective than the saver's credit," said Stephen Roll, assistant professor at Washington University in St. Louis' Brown School and research director at its Center for Social Development. "The saver's credit never reached tax filers at scale." In addition to low awareness of the credit, "low-income households like those targeted by the saver's credit usually owe very little, or even nothing, in taxes, so reducing their tax liability provides them with minimal benefit," Roll said. The new Saver's Match is part of an ongoing broader effort to help workers save for retirement. An estimated 53.7 million full-time and part-time private-sector workers between the ages of 18 and 65 lack access to any employer-based retirement plan, according to 2025 research from the Economic Innovation Group , a bipartisan public policy group. Under the Saver's Match program, single-filer taxpayers with annual modified adjusted gross income up to $20,500 or joint filers earning up to $41,000 can qualify for a government match equal to 50% of retirement contributions up to $2,000, for a maximum yearly match of $1,000 per person. Single filers with annual modified adjusted gross incomes of between $20,501 and $35,499 will qualify for reduced matching contributions, as will joint filers making between $41,001 and $70,999. Other qualifications include being at least age 18, not being a student or someone else's dependent and generally being a U.S. resident for tax purposes. They also must make qualifying retirement contributions. Complications still have to be sorted out However, there are kinks to work out. For example, although Roth IRA contributions count for eligibility, those accounts cannot receive the match. This means that workers who save via a Roth — including nearly all of those enrolled in state-run auto-IRA programs — would need a traditional account to receive the match, experts say. A joint Treasury Department and IRS notice issued Aug. 7 indicates that the agencies are considering a "conduit" traditional IRA that would receive the Saver's Match and then transfer it to a Roth — which would be a taxable conversion. The public can provide input on the notice through Oct. 5. The simpler the program is, the better for taxpayers, said Shai Akabas, vice president of economic policy at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a think tank.

events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Coming soon: our 2026 list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch With the planet nearing 1.5 °C of warming, climate policies being unraveled, and Big Tech backpedaling on its climate ambitions, it can be tempting to give in to climate doom and defeatism. But despite the headwinds, the world has still made incredible progress. That’s why MIT Technology Review publishes its annual list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch . Once a year, we compile a list of 10 companies that we believe have done the most, or have the best chance, to make a real dent in emissions or improve public safety and health. We’ve now finalized our 2026 list and will publish it on October 6. It features companies making strides in energy storage, nuclear power, transportation and other areas despite today’s regressive climate politics. We hope you’ll enjoy the package and perhaps come away feeling a bit more hopeful about our climate’s future. Here’s what to expect . —James Temple Subscribe to receive full access to this year’s list , and keep reading The Download to be among the first to see it. When can we say AI made a scientific discovery? Last week, Anthropic announced that its new molecular biology lab had made its first discovery: its AI agents had flagged a previously uncatalogued pattern surrounding an enzyme, a pattern “reminiscent” of what led to the gene-editing technology CRISPR. But the claims angered biologists. Some questioned whether merely finding the pattern amounted to a discovery at all. Another said his team had already discovered the same pattern, raising questions about whether Anthropic’s system had learned from his conversations with Claude. It’s a reminder that what’s novel for AI may be routine, unsurprising or simply not that consequential to a biologist. And the grand claims could make real progress harder to recognize. events.title: I was laid off from Meta in May. I have a family to support, but I felt prepared — here's my advice to be ready for layoffs.
events.summary: It didn't take Ayodele long to work out his next steps after a layoff. Courtesy of Adekunle Ayodele When layoffs came knocking on Adekunle Ayodele's door, he felt prepared. He had a range of options to turn to, from real estate income to business ideas. "Having options is never a bad thing," Ayodele said, as layoffs in the tech world continue. This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Adekunle Ayodele, 45, who lives in Georgia. The following has been edited for length and clarity. Working at Meta , I knew getting laid off was a possibility. In recent years, layoffs have been happening rapidly in tech, and traditional ideas around job security and the 9-to-5 have been shifting. I was nearly four years into my role as a program manager at Meta when we were notified that layoffs would be happening in a few weeks, on May 20 . At 7 a.m. that morning, I checked my email. No news yet. At 7.02, nothing happened. I kept on refreshing my inbox, and at around 7.14 a.m., I found out my service was no longer needed. My view has always been that if a company decides my skills are no longer required, that's fair. Because of my faith, I believe that everything happens for a reason. My immediate response was to give praise to God, say goodbye to my colleagues, and put my laptop away. I have a wife and two kids I need to provide for. I felt prepared for the layoff because I always tried to live below my means. I also had entrepreneurial ideas in my back pocket. I was ready to figure out my next chapter. It took me two minutes to work out what I wanted to do I'm focusing on my own ventures now. I'm investing in real estate , which is a significant part of my income and helps me sustain my businesses. Before I joined Meta in 2022, I had started my own company, Databox Technologies, to experiment with different product ideas. While at Meta, I started a nonprofit community for African and Black professionals, called Fostr. I've also relaunched an idea I had a long time ago for an app called Mixle, which makes networking and building connections easier. When I shared on LinkedIn that I was choosing to build after being laid off, 22 people reached out who were interested in joining me. It felt incredibly encouraging. I now have a small team of about 15 people working remotely with me across my projects. The team includes contractors, part-time contributors, interns, and advisors. My work at Meta was on a different scale than what I'm doing with my businesses, but I'm still managing priorities and delivering outcomes. The difference is that now I'm closer to the product and customers. I'm also learning how much leverage individuals and small teams now have because of AI. One night, I realized I wanted to rebuild the entire technology stack for Mixle. AI helped me do so much more quickly and cheaply than if I'd had to pay for human labor. Ayodele said he's working more now than he was while at Meta. Courtesy of Adekunle Ayodele It's important to be prepared for layoffs I'm working way more now than I was when I worked at Meta. If I'm not working, I'm sleeping. But it doesn't feel like work because I'm so invested in it. Mixle has started generating revenue, and while I'm open to another job at the right company, my plan is to keep building and growing my business. Big Tech generally pays well, but lifestyle creep can happen, too. I've always tried to live below my means, which meant getting laid off felt like less of a shock. When it comes to layoffs , prepare before you need to. Build relationships, keep your skills relevant, and understand your finances. Building options over many years, like savings, real estate income, and business ventures, is what mattered most when it came to helping to support my family post-layoff. events.title: Journalist ascends to throne in Uganda kingdom after succession dispute
events.summary: Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma succeeds King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who died last month. A journalist has been crowned king of Uganda’s Tooro Kingdom, becoming the 13th monarch of the Batooro people in a ceremony marking the ⁠end of a succession dispute . Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma succeeded King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, whose death last month from cancer at age 34 triggered a feud after his mother said a previously undisclosed son was entitled to the throne. list 1 of 3 Mystery son and disputed heir: Uganda’s king buried amid succession dispute list 2 of 3 A kingdom within a republic: Inside Uganda’s Buganda list 3 of 3 Uganda football star Owori killed, weeks after death of rugby’s Gongodyo Uganda is a ⁠constitutional republic governed by an elected president, but four pre-colonial kingdoms remain influential symbols of identity and heritage despite not having political power. A 21-member committee from the royal Babiito clan selected Kijanangoma, 56, who is Oyo Nyimba’s cousin. Kijanangoma took the royal ‌name Edward Rukidi Nyabongo I in a traditional ceremony that included the slaughter of a bull and sprinkling of a hen’s blood in Tooro’s capital, Fort Portal. Nyabongo I walked to Karuziika Palace from midnight to 3am on Tuesday (21:00 GMT on Monday to 00:00 GMT on Tuesday) before taking part in a mock battle for the crown. Former colleagues of Nyabongo ⁠I at the state broadcaster UBC, where he worked as a news anchor and editor, described him as humble and down to earth. The selection of Nyabongo I as king was widely contested because he wasn’t in the direct line of succession, and the coronation took place despite objections from Oyo Nyimba’s mother, Best Kemigisa, and sister, Princess Ruth Komuntale. They say the late king left behind a young son and a will ‌naming him as his heir. The claim to the throne has led to increasing disquiet within the community on the selection of Nyabongo I. The reason for Kemigisa’s withholding of the identity of the heir remains unclear. Critics said, however, that Oyo’s alleged child would have to have been introduced to the kingdom’s elders when his father was still alive to become a legitimate heir, if he even exists at all.

events.title: 83% of CFOs say U.S. stocks are overvalued, even as optimism about their companies rises
events.summary: Good morning. CFOs are feeling better about their own companies even as they become more cautious about markets and the broader economy. And concern is growing about the technology they’re racing to deploy.  Deloitte’s Q3 2026 CFO Signals survey , which polled 200 North American finance chiefs at companies with at least $1 billion in revenue, found that the CFO Confidence Score climbed to 6.1 from 5.9 last quarter, moving back into “high” territory. Ninety percent of respondents said they were more optimistic about their companies’ financial prospects, even as risk appetite cooled slightly, with 53% saying now is a good time to take greater risks, down from 59% in Q2. But Ed Hardy, U.S. financial services leader at Deloitte, noted that CFOs’ views on the relative attractiveness of debt and equity financing changed little. More striking to Hardy was the gap between how CFOs view their own businesses and how they view the broader market. There was a sharp increase in the share of CFOs who believe U.S. equity markets are overvalued: 83%, compared with 49% in Q2. Despite that, equity attractiveness remained flat in Q3, while debt attractiveness increased four percentage points. “If they feel it’s overvalued, buying might not be the most objective thing to do,” Hardy told me, adding that elevated valuations are prompting finance chiefs to “search for the highest use of capital,” which is a dynamic he connects to rising investment in AI. AI and technology are also becoming a growing source of both opportunity and risk. Technology deployment, including generative AI, was among CFOs’ leading internal concerns, while cybersecurity topped the external-risk list at 50%. Hardy said the two are closely linked. “AI probably starts to increase your already heightened concern around cyber,” he said, pointing to the growing use of open platforms and third-party models. Meanwhile, CFOs’ 12-month outlook for the North American economy slipped slightly but remained generally steady compared with Q2. Inflation, supply chain disruption and the economy itself ranked among their leading external concerns, trailing cybersecurity. Survey data collection started Aug. 24 and wrapped Sept. 8, before the Federal Reserve’s Sept. 16 rate decision , leaving open how CFO sentiment might shift in the next quarter. “You always wonder whether it’s embedded into the psyche of where they think the market’s going,” Hardy said. He added that he’ll be watching closely to see whether economic and geopolitical uncertainty eases into 2027. Looking ahead to 2027, Hardy said he expects CFOs to keep pushing AI “beyond experiment into really grounded applications,” while wrestling with governance, shifting token-based pricing models and how to measure real benefits. “The CFO role is increasing in being a convener across the enterprise,” he said, as finance takes on broader oversight of AI’s costs and outcomes. events.title: Alaska Airlines is doubling down on premium travel. Take a look at its newest long-haul cabins.
events.summary: Aurora Suites on 737 Max 10. Alaska Air Group Alaska Air Group announced new Premium Reserve seating on Alaska and Hawaiian Airlines flights. Perks will include reclining seats with leg and calf rests, 38 inches of pitch, and upgraded dining. It also announced upgraded business-class and lie-flat seats on some Boeing 737 Max 10s. Alaska Air Group is the latest US air carrier to shore up its premium seating offerings — part of an industry-wide boom to cater to passengers who will pay more for premium perks. On Tuesday, Alaska Air Group, which operates Alaska Airlines and Hawaiian Airlines , unveiled a new premium economy cabin called "Premium Reserve" and upgraded business-class suites. These will fly on mostly long-haul flights to Europe and Asia, and on select domestic routes. Since acquiring Hawaiian for nearly $2 billion in 2024, Alaska has been pursuing its "Alaska Accelerate" plan to expand its premium offerings and international presence from its Seattle hub . The latest cabins are part of that strategy, making Alaska increasingly look like a major global carrier rather than the largely domestic airline it was once known as. "We believe premium is more than a seat," Ben Minicucci, CEO of Alaska Air Group, said in a statement. "It's how guests feel from the moment they book their trip to the moment they arrive at the airport, to when they're in the air with us." A new premium cabin and lie-flat seats on 737 Max 10s Available to book on both airlines starting next summer, Alaska and Hawaiian's new premium economy will feature wide reclining seats with leg and calf rests and a pitch — or the distance from one seat to the seat in front of it — of 38 inches, It will also include a 16-inch, Bluetooth-capable screen, outlets and USB-C charging ports, and upgraded in-flight dining menus. A rendering of Alaska Airlines' Premium Reserve seating on a Boeing 737-10 Max. Alaska Air Group Alaska already offers a premium-economy-like cabin called Premium Class, but the cabin type will be a first for Hawaiian. Premium Reserve will be available on Alaska's 787 and select 737 Max 10 aircraft, as well as Hawaiian's A330 fleet, with flights beginning in 2028. Alaska doesn't yet have the Max 10, which was nearing the finish line for certification after years of delays tied to safety and quality concerns. But CNBC reported on Monday that regulators have again delayed certification due to a newly discovered software issue. Beyond premium economy, lie-flat business class — called "Aurora Suites" on Alaska and "Leihōkū Suites" on Hawaiian to retain each airline's distinct branding — has gotten a refresh. A rendering of Hawaiian Airlines' refreshed business class. Alaska Air Group Hawaiian's Leihōkū Suite, its 787 business-class product, serves select routes to Asia, Oceania, and North America. It will be added to the A330 and feature "hotel-quality bedding and enhanced onboard amenities." Alaska's Aurora Suites will be deployed on all 787 Dreamliners and include upgraded upholstery and materials. Both suites will have sliding doors, Bluetooth, big inflight screens, and access to airport lounges. Aurora will also be installed on 737 Max 10 planes flying select transcontinental routes, joining the increasing number of airline narrowbody planes with lie-flat premium seats. A rendering of the new Alaska business-class coming to its 737 Max fleet. Alaska Air Group These premium cabins won't be cheap. A round-trip business-class flight from Seattle to Tokyo in mid-March is about $6,500 on Alaska; the same seat to London is about $5,300. Basic economy is about one-fifth of each of those business-class fares. Alaska is also facing fierce competition. It's up against legacy US carriers with already massive widebody fleets, extensive international networks, and well-established premium products. Alaska knows it's playing catch-up. "I think where you're seeing strength with the legacy carriers is in the premium space and in the international space," Minicucci said in an April 2026 earnings call. "And if you look at our strategy under Alaska Accelerate, that's exactly where we're leaning into." Courting passengers who pay a premium In post-COVID air travel , US airlines are moving away from packing as many people as possible into economy to increase revenue. Instead, they are pivoting toward customers who will spend more on premium travel experiences, such as airline lounges and higher-tier in-flight amenities. A McKinsey analysis published in June found that on transatlantic wide-body flights, business-class cabins are earning almost as much as economy cabins, even though they carry far fewer passengers. That premium demand has remained despite rising oil prices and soaring airfares amid the war in Iran, partly buoyed by continued spending from more affluent travelers. "The folks who are more oriented towards purchasing into our premium cabins have been super resilient," Minicucci said in a 2025 earnings call. A rendering of Hawaiian Airlines' Premium Reserve seating on an Airbus A330. Alaska Air Group United Airlines' director of onboard products and partnerships, Peter Wolkowski, told Business Insider during the UK's Farnborough Airshow in July that premium economy is its fastest-growing cabin on the company's 787 fleet. In 2025, Delta's premium revenue increased 7% year-over-year, while its main cabin revenue decreased. On an earnings call in October 2025, then-Delta president Glen Hauenstein predicted that premium revenue was expected to exceed Main Cabin revenue by 2027. "When you think about what's different and what's changed over the last 10 or 15 years, the premium products used to be loss leaders, and now they're the highest-margin products," he said. Super Heavy had problems of its own. All 33 Raptor 3 engines ignited at 07:48 CT, but one shut down during ascent. The booster later reignited 26 of the 28 engines planned for its boostback maneuver. During descent, it reignited 11 of the planned 13 engines for the high-thrust portion of its landing burn before stepping down to five and then three. It splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico, after which its flight termination system was deliberately triggered to test the safety hardware. More consequential was the premature shutdown of one of Starship's three vacuum-optimized Raptors during ascent. The remaining five engines burned longer to compensate, leaving the spacecraft on its planned suborbital trajectory. This ensured it would return to Earth even if controllers lost control, but also meant a further burn was required to enter orbit. Controllers then had to decide whether enough propulsion redundancy remained to perform both the orbital insertion maneuver and, crucially, the later deorbit burn. According to SpaceX , all three sea-level Raptors remained healthy, so controllers gave the go-ahead to relight one and complete the climb to orbit. After deploying the satellites, Starship began its coast around Earth, but controllers cut short most of the intended ten-hour flight "out of an abundance of caution." It performed its deorbit burn and splashed down in the North Pacific after about three hours. Unlike the Flight 13 vehicle, which survived its landing and was recovered, this one toppled over and exploded shortly after hitting the water. Reaching orbit, deploying an operational payload, and executing a controlled deorbit represent major advances for Starship. However the premature Raptor shutdown remains a concern given the launch cadence required for a lunar landing. NASA's inspector general said SpaceX's lunar architecture calls for a propellant depot followed by more than ten tanker launches, potentially at intervals of about six days. SpaceX has yet to demonstrate vehicle-to-vehicle propellant transfer in orbit. That tanker campaign is not required for the revised Artemis III mission in 2027, which is now a docking demonstration in low Earth orbit rather than a lunar landing. SpaceX's contribution will be a single Version 3 Starship fitted with a docking system so that Orion can rendezvous with it; astronauts will remain aboard Orion. Mantil was most recently a Goldman partner and global head of the bank's ETF accelerator, its in-house platform that helped clients launch investment products. "The opportunity to join Polymarket is a rare chance to help shape an exploding asset class at an inflection point in its development," Mantil said in a release. "I've spent my career guiding institutions as they adopt new products and enter new markets, and I look forward to bringing that expertise to Polymarket as we build the institutional business and expand the role prediction markets can play across investment and risk-management strategies." Mantil is the latest hire by Polymarket as it continues to expand following the official launch of its U.S. exchange in May . CNBC reported in August on a slew of new hires across both Polymarket's international and domestic platforms, and the company announced earlier this month that it was hiring Warren Jenson as its chief financial officer. Jenson previously held roles at companies such as including Amazon and Delta Air Lines . Prediction markets — which have seen their volumes surge in the past year primarily due to retail traders interested in their sports-related offerings — are increasingly looking to attract institutional liquidity to their platforms . Polymarket CEO and founder Shayne Coplan said in the release that Mantil is the right person to lead the latest expansion of the company's business. "Lisa's experience and relationships across the institutional world are world class," Coplan said. Institutional adoption of prediction markets is still in early stages, and some players are staying on the sidelines as platforms are in a regulatory brawl with states regarding who has the right to oversee their sports-related event contracts. But that hasn't stopped platforms from trying to woo large traders. Rival Kalshi in April became the first exchange to complete a block trade , which are large transactions negotiated privately to avoid price volatility that are typical on Wall Street. Polymarket's international platform, which is not regulated in the U.S. and operates on the Polygon blockchain, conducted its first block trade one month later. Brokers working with early institutional participants on prediction markets have told CNBC that the company has had discussions about completing block trades on its U.S. exchange, and is nearing the ability to do so. Polymarket declined to comment regarding the status of block trades on its domestic platform. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

events.title: ChatGPT's ads are a lot like San Francisco’s infamous billboards
events.summary: Highway 101 in San Francisco. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images A new report from Graphite shows the dominance of B2B software in ChatGPT's advertising. OpenAI is now more than 6 months into its ads push, and says it hit a $1 billion run rate. Graphite has positive news for the AI company: less than half of ad-eligible users are seeing ads. San Francisco's stretch of Highway 101 is infamous for billboards that peddle wonky software to other tech companies. ChatGPT, invented nearby, is so far more of the same. Ads pitching business software to corporate buyers made up the largest category of ad impressions on ChatGPT from March to August at almost 20%, a new study by marketing agency Graphite found. Another 8.5% of ChatGPT ad impressions in the period promoted business and professional services and 4.6% plugged developer tools, according to the report, which analyzed Similarweb user data. OpenAI launched ads on its main AI service in February and is trying to grow the business into a meaningful revenue stream before its planned initial public offering next year. Some good news for Sam Altman : Graphite found that the click-through rate for ChatGPT ads more than doubled from late March to early September, indicating the company is doing a better job of targeting. And less than half of ad-eligible users have been served an ad at all. "There's a lot of upside, or there's a lot more reach that they can hit," Ethan Smith, Graphite's CEO, told Business Insider. ChatGPT ads have a SaaS-sales tilt OpenAI says the ads it places on ChatGPT are relevant to the conversation a user is having with the chatbot. The company also bars certain categories, such as legal services, politics, and gambling. So far, many of the biggest advertisers are software companies, Graphite's report shows. Monday.com and HubSpot were among the advertisers that appeared most often in the data, along with Resume.io and Canva. The form builder site Jotform, another top advertiser, ran more than 930 varieties of ChatGPT ads in just a month, Graphite found. The agency noticed a fair amount of fluctuation when it looked at companies over time. HubSpot and Canva each advertised in a burst before trailing off over the summer. Some companies, like Zapier and the Wall Street Journal, dropped off entirely by the end of the reporting period. Cursor, the AI coding company acquired earlier this year by SpaceX, also advertised heavily on ChatGPT, according to the Similarweb data. Smith said the presence of Cursor and other AI tool providers like Speechify among the top ChatGPT advertisers is easy to explain: if you're using a chatbot, you're more likely to use those other tools, too. "It's self-selecting people who are necessarily AI-forward," he said. OpenAI's ads business is still in flux At a Goldman Sachs conference in early September, OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar said the company's ads team is still working on the basics of the product, including figuring out pricing and deploying it globally. She said the business had hit $1 billion mark in annual run-rate revenue. "We're starting to really see some strong outcomes for advertisers who care about performance," Friar said. "And this is all before we've really launched a format that feels truly endemic to AI. That's what I get super excited about." It isn't totally clear what an AI-native ad format would look like, but Friar said she'd like the ads product to eventually be like " if Google and Meta had a baby ." Meta and Google have huge amounts of demographic data on their users. As OpenAI tries to figure out how to make its ads more valuable, Smith thinks the company has room for optimism. "I suspect that the targeting is much harder here and will probably improve much more over time and might become, perhaps, hyper-relevant," he said. Have a tip? events.title: ADP: what 77 years of payroll taught us about AI
events.summary: The promise of artificial intelligence in payroll and HR is straightforward: fewer manual processes, faster decisions and greater efficiency. But there is a risk in moving too quickly. If a company automates a flawed process or removes the human expertise that catches exceptions, it doesn’t eliminate errors. In fact, it scales them. Payroll is a good example. Employees expect to be paid accurately and on time. Employers need to comply with a growing number of regulations, often across multiple jurisdictions. It’s a complex system that must be correct all of the time. That tension between innovation and execution has shaped ADP for nearly eight decades. We helped pioneer the payroll services industry when businesses were still managing payroll by hand. As the industry evolved, we helped move payroll from manual processing to automated service delivery, were among the first to bring payroll to the cloud and helped make workforce information available through mobile technology. We later created an online marketplace that connected clients with a broader ecosystem of workforce solutions. Our business evolved as the workforce evolved. What began with a single small business in New Jersey grew into a company supporting more than 1.1 million clients in more than 140 countries. Each step brought new capabilities, but the underlying challenge remained the same: making those capabilities work for businesses with different needs, different workforces and increasingly complex requirements. That history has reinforced a simple lesson: technology can change how work gets done, but expertise is what makes it work in practice. AI can help, but payroll has little room for error Today’s businesses face growing complexity from every direction. They’re managing employees across countries and work models while adapting to changing labor laws, pay transparency requirements, evolving privacy expectations and the responsible use of AI. And payroll professionals feel the weight. According to ADP’s Potential of Payroll 2026 research, 75% of payroll leaders say keeping up with local regulations is a significant challenge, 68% report incurring penalties for noncompliance once or twice a year, and 69% say they sometimes overpay employees rather than risk a compliance violation. To help alleviate the weight, the transformative potential of AI and automation continue to be at the forefront of payroll leaders’ minds. Around half of the organizations surveyed have automated core processes like data collection (52%), data entry (49%), reconciliations (47%) and reporting (49%). Though as they look for ways to drive efficiency, they recognize the importance of adopting AI responsibly, balancing progress with compliance and the employee experience. In order to use AI effectively and accurately, businesses must first determine where AI fits, how it should be governed and when human expertise needs to step in. If businesses rush to automate, they risk overlooking the critical layer of human oversight needed in AI-driven HR. Such an oversight could lead to payroll and compliance issues before AI delivers any efficiency gains. Leading the teams that support our clients every day has reinforced for me that new capabilities work best when they make experienced people better at their jobs. AI can surface relevant information, identify patterns and automate routine work. People still need to understand the context, recognize an exception and know when an answer doesn’t make sense. The value in AI is helping people find information faster, streamline routine work and respond more efficiently to questions. The goal is to give people better tools and more time to focus on the issues that require human judgment. That distinction matters in payroll and HR, innately human functions, where a seemingly small exception can have significant consequences on people at work. Human expertise provides the context and accountability that automated systems cannot. Global complexity demands more than technology A global payroll transformation can look straightforward from a distance: implement new software, move the data and turn the system on. In practice, it is far more complicated. Every country brings its own tax rules, employment laws, reporting requirements and local practices. Those requirements change, and the systems supporting them have to change with them. The real work is making sure the entire operation functions together while accounting for the rules and requirements in each country. That is where experience makes a difference. Software can connect those markets, but people still need to understand payroll, regulation and local requirements, recognize when something doesn’t look right and determine what needs to happen next. Bringing those capabilities together allows a complex operation to keep moving as conditions change. That’s also what clients tell us they value. They want tools that make their work easier, but they also want to know that someone understands what happens when a regulation changes, an exception surfaces or something goes wrong. Even as technology advances, businesses still want to know there’s someone behind the system who can effectively help when a problem comes up. The next chapter: AI + expertise AI will continue to reshape workforce management, automating routine work, identifying patterns and creating new ways to support employees and managers. The companies that gain the most from these capabilities will understand where automation can take over, where human expertise needs to intervene and how to make the two work together. They’ll prioritize the human oversight required to realize the valuable outcomes of AI-driven HR. This is the lesson ADP has learned over decades of technology and change. We have moved from paper-based payroll to automated processing, from on-premise systems to the cloud, from desktop applications to mobile technology and now to AI. The technology has changed dramatically. The responsibility has not. The opportunity ahead is to apply AI where it solves real problems for businesses, designing around how their workforces operate today and adapting as their needs change. In an AI-powered world of work, that means pairing new capabilities with the experience to know where those capabilities can deliver the most value. Employers still need to pay people accurately. They still need to comply with the rules. They still need someone to help when something goes wrong. Supporting people at work is still the overarching goal of HR. The industry’s next era will depend on using AI to make those responsibilities easier to manage for the humans in charge.
