events.title: The residents and wind farm on the frontline of Australia's energy wars
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mount Fox residents say they bear brunt of net zero as wind farm construction to begin The locality of Mount Fox was named after the iconic crater of an inactive 100,000-year-old volcano. ( Supplied: Keep Mount Fox Wild ) Construction will soon begin on the nation's largest wind farm to be built in two years, but frustrated residents say they are bearing the brunt of Australia's push for net zero. The Gawara Baya wind farm includes 68 turbines and a 100-megawatt battery spread over 148 hectares near the 100,000-year-old dormant volcano Mount Fox in north Queensland. Danish investors Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) acquired the project from WindLab earlier this month, announcing funding was ready and construction would begin "imminently". Energy experts say the development is a breakthrough towards the federal government's 2030 renewables goal. The 100,000-year-old dormant volcano Mount Fox rises from the surrounding bushland near Ingham. ( ABC News: James Tugwell ) Mount Fox near Ingham has about 84 residents and neighbours the world heritage listed Wet Tropics. There is a campground with a concrete cricket pitch, road signs warning motorists about cassowaries, and a primary school with a mob of emus and three students. "I wake up every morning and there's big trees and open spaces and all you hear is nature in all its diversity," resident Kim Armstrong said. Kim Armstrong is opposed to the windfarm development. ( ABC News: James Tugwell ) The closest turbine will be about 5 kilometres from the Wet Tropics border. Ms Armstrong said she was worried about the impact of the 140-metre turbines on the region's biodiversity, human and environmental health, run-off onto the Great Barrier Reef and what would happen to the turbines after their 35-year life cycle. "I don't think a lot of Australians really understand exactly what it takes to put a wind farm up and the destruction that it causes," she said. A wind-powered relic at Mount Fox. ( ABC News: James Tugwell ) Ms Armstrong said Mount Fox residents were on the frontline of Australia's energy wars, pursuing the "dream" of net zero because of political decisions made 2,000 kilometres away in Canberra by people she did not vote for. She said people in cities thought "we have to do this for climate change" and resisting labelled her a "climate denier". "That's not the case at all," she said. Some Mount Fox residents say net zero is a dream ruining their idyllic home. ( ABC News: James Tugwell ) Ms Armstrong founded community group Keep Mount Fox Wild, which she said included about half of the town's residents. "There are several wind farms earmarked for up here. We just don't want them," she said. CIP project CEO Mark Branson said the project met strict government regulations. "We understand that not everybody in the region is a fan of wind farms and this is always the case," he said. A sign opposing wind turbines in the kitchenette of the Mount Fox campground. ( ABC News: James Tugwell ) "But we know we have a really good foundation for the project in terms of the rigorous environmental assessment that has been done, all the community consultation that's been done, all the engagement with the local businesses and councils." He said construction would create about 500 jobs, with most workers to be housed at an onsite village. Mr Branson said Gawara Baya was paving the way for new wind projects to replace aging coal assets. "Projects like Gawara Baya are really critical in making sure we've got enough electricity to feed into the grid and power people's homes, to power industry and make sure we've got stable electricity supply into the future," he said. A map of the planned locations of the 68 windfarms near Mount Fox. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins ) This project is the first wind farm to reach construction under the federal government's Capacity Investment Scheme and represents a breaking of a deadlock, according to Grattan Institute climate and energy program director Alison Reeve. "The hope of the industry is that this project is a sign that that pipeline is finally moving and that this is going to be the first of quite a lot of projects, particularly on the east coast, that will now start to get built," Ms Reeve said. Alison Reeve says the Gawara Baya project is the biggest to reach financial close under the Capacity Investment Scheme. ( ABC News ) Under the scheme, which aims to help achieve the target of 82 per cent renewables by 2030, the government guarantees the price for electricity, subsidising the producer if electricity prices fall and sharing in profits if prices rise above a certain price.

events.title: The US-China tectonic plates have shifted
events.summary: Before this week, the last time a US president greeted a foreign leader at Joint Base Andrews was when John F. Kennedy welcomed British Prime Minister Harold Macmillan in 1962. But that’s not the reason the image of US President Donald Trump waiting at the foot of the stairs of an Air China Boeing-747 to personally greet Chinese leader Xi Jinping is historic. Macmillan led a close American ally; Xi leads America’s paramount adversary. In rolling out the red carpet, Trump underscored how rapidly the balance of power in the relationship has shifted. The turning point came last year, when China made the ultimate power move, threatening to choke off rare earths — and turn US factories dark — after Trump ramped up tariffs on Chinese goods to more than 140%. Trump backed down, and at the time, Rush Doshi, a Georgetown University professor and former Biden administration official, wrote that China had proved itself to be a “ true peer ” of the US, unafraid to push back. Doshi’s take on the arrival ceremony, which also included a 21-gun salute and a flyover by B-1B bombers — far exceeding courtesies extended to Trump in Beijing in May — has been that China believes “they’ve basically tamed the United States.” “The tectonic plates have shifted beneath us,” he told me, “and both leaders are acting accordingly.” The China scholar Orville Schell writes that the US’ epic diplomatic successes of the 20th century — securing the unconditional surrender of Japan and Germany after World War Two; defusing the Cuban missile crisis; securing arms-control agreements with Moscow to wind down the Cold War — set an unrealistic ceiling for Americans about what’s achievable today. This summit established a new, lower floor. In classic diplomacy, protocol giveaways are supposed to be reciprocated by substantive concessions. Otherwise, why bother? Xi offered two pandas — Ping Ping and Fu Shuang — for the Atlanta zoo, bromides on how the US and China must “coexist in peace” and, according to Trump, showed interest in the granite used to construct the new White House helipad. Yet at the same time, China is supplying Russia with dual-use technology to pummel Ukraine, and as Xi landed, The Wall Street Journal was reporting details of how Beijing had supplied Iran with rocket propellant and electronic components used to make drones and missiles that Tehran is using to lash out at its neighbors — and reportedly kill US service personnel — in the Gulf. As for actual results, there was talk of an AI hotline to notify each other of risks that rise to the national security level, and an agreement to extend a trade truce for two months. But again, reality belies the rhetoric: It’s far from clear that China and the US assess AI risks in the same way — and whether a hotline would actually work . Moreover, the short extension of the trade armistice only underscores its fragility; Beijing is still squeezing flows of rare earths to extract concessions from the US and coerce its allies, including Japan. It’s worth remembering that, until quite recently, US and Chinese leaders aired their disagreements in front of TV cameras at joint news conferences on issues ranging from human rights to market access for foreign companies, with American presidents pressing for concessions. This week, by contrast, has been an exercise in shallow bonhomie. Even a few Republican loyalists have recoiled at the extravagant pageantry, seemingly designed to flatter Xi and awe a domestic audience, although the absence of TV cameras at the Rose Garden ceremony undermined that low-ambition objective. Ahead of the summit, Roger Wicker, the Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman, questioned why Trump was offering such a “lavish welcome” to a “brutal, unelected, and oppressive dictator.” After a state dinner featuring bok choy and sesame-crusted sea bass — and a clutch of tech moguls including Tim Cook, Elon Musk, and Jensen Huang — the puzzle remains: Why did Trump blow diplomatic capital for such meager results? “Tremendous things will be happening,” Trump posted on Friday. That’s a diplomatic hope, not a deliverable.

events.title: Trump says he rejected the latest Iranian proposal
events.summary: President Trump said on Saturday that he rejected the latest Iranian proposal that was conveyed to the U.S. during indirect negotiations in New York this week. Why it matters: While Qatar and other regional mediators are trying to revive negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, the gaps on the key issues are still very wide. While Iran wants to focus any talks on the Strait of Hormuz and the U.S. naval blockade, the Trump administration demands the Iranians agree to nuclear concessions. What he is saying: "They have made a proposal and I rejected it," Trump said. But a U.S. official claimed "positive and constructive" discussions are still ongoing between the U.S. and Iran through the mediators, including on nuclear issues. Driving the news: U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a new round of indirect negotiations with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this week. Qatari officials participated in the negotiations, passing messages between the two parties, sources with direct knowledge said. Araghchi gave Witkoff and Kushner Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and resuming nuclear talks. Iran proposed reopening the strait and resuming nuclear talks in a week, if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade, removes sanctions on oil sales and reinstates a ceasefire across the region. The U.S. negotiators made it clear to the Iranians during the talks on Tuesday that Iran doesn't control the strait and therefore can't make demands about it, a source told Axios. State of play: Dozens of oil tankers are transiting the strait each day under U.S. protection, moving millions of barrels of oil to global markets — still well below pre-war volumes but enough to ease some pressure. U.S. officials claim that over the last 72 hours around 60 million barrels of oil transited through the Strait of Hormuz.
